utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you, for the first time in 2015, call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. The Chamber was informed that there are two matters to be raised by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Good morning. I wanted to raise these two matters as -- before these housekeeping matters started mounting up. They're relatively simple. The first one is simply that the B/C/S version of P3758 was uploaded into e-court in the incorrect order, although the English translation is in the correct chronological order. Accordingly, we have re-uploaded the document under 65 ter 03078a, this time with the B/C/S document in correct chronological order. If the Defence are therefore in agreement, we would request that 65 ter number 03078a be assigned P3758.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Defence, any objections? No objections. I take it that you would like to have 03078 be replaced by 03078a in the B/C/S version.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, you are hereby instructed to replace the current B/C/S version of P3758 by the newly uploaded one, which is 65 ter 03078a. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And for the second matter, Mr. President, I think we could deal with it more clearly and cleanly if we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. And although I have an agenda of 17 items still to be dealt with, I'll deal with only one as -- of some urgency at this very moment. It's about the scheduling of the remaining Defence case and the request for an update on expert reports. The Chamber has now heard approximately one-third of the witnesses the Defence intends to call, according to its witness list of the 19th of May of 2014. The Defence has also used less than one-third of the time it was granted by the Chamber in the decision of the 12th of May, 2014. If the current pace is sustained, the Defence case will continue into 2016. In order to assist the Chamber in making accurate projections, the Defence is invited to advise the Chamber as soon as possible whether it intends to drop any witnesses from its witness list, even if that will be only a preliminary indication. I can imagine, Mr. Lukic, that you have -- do not have an immediate answer to that, but you certainly will have thought about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You're absolutely right, Your Honour, on both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. When could we hear from you to hear the result of your thinking, especially on the second matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I -- can we deal with that next week, so we have this weekend to maybe go through the list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Early -- beginning of next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. You have got until after the weekend to -- to further rethink what you have thought about already. Now, some of the remaining Defence witnesses are expert witnesses, and I -- meanwhile, I already invite the usher to escort the next witness into the courtroom. But some of the remaining Defence witnesses are expert witnesses. As of today's date, the Defence has not filed any expert reports. It's now becoming urgent to start the Rule 94 bis procedure for these witnesses. On the 5th of June of last year, the Chamber instructed the Defence to file monthly updates on the progress of expert reports. The Chamber did not receive any reports in November and December, and the Chamber therefore requests the Defence to review the situation with regard to the expert reports and be ready to provide a detailed report in court on the 26th of January, 2015. I leave it to that for the time being. The next witness the Defence calls is --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And my colleague Stojanovic will lead this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mrs. Karlica. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Ms. Karlica, you'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find Mr. Stojanovic to your left behind the lectern. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mrs. Karlica.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to ask you to tell us your exact name and surname. Slowly, please.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Zdravka Karlica.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Karlica, at one point in time did you answer questions that were put to you by the Defence of General Mladic and did you provide a statement in writing?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have 65 ter 1D01672 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, there is a screen before you and there is a text entitled: "Witness Statement." Now, this is what I'm asking you: On this page of this witness statement, can you recognise this signature of yours?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please take a look at the last page of this document now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Madam, on this last page after the text entitled "Witness Acknowledgement," can you recognise your own signature and the date that we see on this page? Is it written in your own hand?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now please take a look at paragraph 1 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zdravka, while preparing for your testimony in court, as we went through this statement of yours, did you indicate to me that it would be more precise and better to have the penultimate sentence changed in paragraph 1, the one that says: "I have been doing this job for 13 years." Should it say: "I have been doing this work for 13 years"? Because you're not actually employed by this NGO.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In your view, would it be more precise, for the record, for this sentence to read as follows: "I have been doing this work for 13 years"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I would like us to take a look at paragraph 6 of this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In the first paragraph in paragraph 6 in the last sentence, during proofing, you also pointed out an imprecision to me. So instead of the word "paternal uncle," it should say "maternal uncle," "stric," "ujak"?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So, for the record, should this sentence read as follows: "After the murder of Radenko Djapa, his maternal uncle retaliated against the Muslims for his murder," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to ask that we take a look at paragraph 16 of your statement. In the last sentence, did you indicate to me that a correction should be made? In the last line, we see the last name Zgonjanin but should it say Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, should this sentence read as follows then: "My late husband was with one of his soldiers, Zeljko Zgonjanin, and he was the first to see that someone had hurled a grenade from the room next door at Zoran at him. Zoran just managed to say, 'watch out, it's on bomb,' and he immediately through himself to the ground. However, the grenade exploded between his legs and blew to pieces his left thigh, and Skrbic sustained wounds to both legs."

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now that we've made these three corrections in your statement, today in this courtroom, after you have taken solemn declaration, would you give identical answers to questions put to you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And would the statement stated in such precise terms contain everything that you were asked about, to the best of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mrs. Zdravka.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender the statement of Witness Zdravka Karlica, 65 ter 1D01672.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any objections by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Good morning. No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zec. Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1672 receives number D863, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, this is a good opportunity for me to tender associate exhibits 65 ter numbers 1D02850 - I'm actually tendering three documents - then 1D03511, and 1D16510.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The last one is a 65 ter number without 1D, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's at least how it was announced in Annex B to the motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, that's right. That's right, Your Honour. 65 ter 16510. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, objections against any of the three?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, 1D02850 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D864, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. 1D3511 would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D865, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted. And 65 ter 16510 would receive?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Number D866, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. With your leave, Your Honours, I would like to read a short summary of Witness Zdravka Karlica's statement. Zdravka Karlica is the president of the organisation of the families of POWs and fallen soldiers and missing civilians of Prijedor municipality. She has been doing this work for 13 years now. When the war started, she was in Prijedor where she lived with her family. Immediately after the war broke out in the territory of the former Yugoslavia, her late husband was mobilised and deployed in Croatia as a reserve officer and a member of the JNA. On the 3rd of January 1992, he was wounded and hospitalised in Prijedor where he was when the war started in Bosnia and Herzegovina. He was then mobilised and asked to report to the Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks. He was then assigned to the JNA units which were deployed in Prijedor. From conversations with her husband, she learnt about a lot of events and incidents that had preceded the breakout of war in Prijedor municipality. She says that the first incident in Prijedor was the murder of the policeman Radenko Djapa who was killed by Muslim extremists. That incident caused a lot of unrest among the general public and population in Prijedor. Her late husband participated in the negotiations in Kozarac in the attempt to resolve the crisis in a nonviolent manner. He told her that the problem with the negotiations was how to disarm paramilitaries that existed in Kozarac. The moderate SDA stream agreed for those units to be disarmed and that postponed a conflict. However, the other elements, extreme elements, did not accept that agreement and, as a result, there was an attack on the military vehicles' column that was moving from the direction of Kozarac. The witness also speaks about the incident which happened on the 22nd of May, 1992 in the village of Hambarine. Her late husband participated in those events, and he also participated in the negotiations with the representative of the Muslim side, Aziz Aliskovic. They discussed the takeover of the dead bodies of VRS members. Finally, the negotiations came to fruition after a couple of hours. The witness also speaks about what she knows of the attack on the central part of town of Prijedor during the night between the 29th and the 30th of May, 1992, and she also speaks about the objectives of that attacked launched by paramilitary formations. Her husband and some of his fellow combatants were wounded during that attack. Due to the severity of his wounds, he was first treated in Banja Luka and then he was transferred to Belgrade where he succumbed to his wounds on the 6th of June, 1992. The witness also shares her immediate knowledge about the departure of the non-Serbian population from Prijedor. She also says that a large number of Muslims left the municipality even before the war. And, finally, she says that in her late husband's units there were members of all nationalities, some of whom were his closest associates. Thank you, Your Honours. This is a short summary of the witness's statement, and with your leave, I would like to put a couple of questions to the witness in order to clarify some matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do so, Mr. Stojanovic. You said it was a short summary. I would say it was a summary. And one of my good intentions was not to intervene before it turned out to be necessary. Perhaps, what was on my mind, I should have reminded you that summaries should be short summaries. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm interested in paragraph 17 of the witness's statement, which is now D863.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Zdravka, in paragraph 17, you pointed out in your statement that you knew what the objectives of Slavko Ecimovic's group had been when they launched the attack on the 29th and the 30th of May, 1992. You mentioned those objectives. How do you know that? Where does your information come from?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: On the 30th of May, my husband was wounded, which means that people from that unit came and told me that the attack had been launched from various directions. He was wounded close to the hotel. Allegedly, that group was supposed to reach Radio Prijedor. That was the main objective. And then the others would have become involved in the fighting around Prijedor. In other words, I heard that from the people who came to our house.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 18 of your statement, you say that the villagers of Cela and Puharska were not bothered and that they remained living in their villages throughout the war. Please tell the Court whether you learned at any point in time that on the eve of the Dayton Accords the villagers of those villages abandoned their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I must say that before 1995, i.e., after Operation Storm, they abandoned their homes because people arrived from Croatia and looked for their new homes. It was only then when they left the villages of Cela and Puharska; but since then a lot of them have returned, as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. And now I would like to draw your attention to paragraph 8 in your statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to move into private session for the next question that I would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Karlica, thank you very much for your answers on behalf of General Mladic's Defence. At this point, we have no further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Before I would invite the Prosecution to start its cross-examination, I would have one question about a paragraph which was specifically addressed by Mr. Stojanovic. In paragraph 18 of your statement, Witness, you said that no one bothered the non-Serbian villages that had not attacked the Serbian forces, and that none of their inhabitants -- that were touched upon and that they remained in their villages throughout the war, and you mentioned two villages. Now, could you tell us what happened with the mothers and the children and the elderly in those villages that had attacked the Serbian forces? I'm not talking about men being involved in the attacks, but I'm talking about their families. Were they -- did anyone touch upon any of those inhabitants - again - of the villages that did attack the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I must admit that I didn't know much about that. There was a meeting in Sehovac near Sanski Most attended by Serbs and Bosniaks from Prijedor. That was the first time I heard that a lot of women and children had been killed around Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did that meeting take place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps six or seven years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, what did you mean when you said that you learned that women and children were killed? Were they intentionally killed, were they murdered, or were they victims of the war operations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, it was a shocking piece of information for me. I heard that 256 women and 10 girls had been killed during the war. That's what I heard on that occasion. On returning from that meeting, together with my colleague who had also attended the meeting, I went to that cemetery to see where so many people had --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, that's not an answer to my question. My question is whether did you learn that they were killed, murdered, or that they were victims of the war operations? If you shell a certain area, it can be that a woman or a child is hit by that. You can also just murder children and women. What did you learn at that meeting that had happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At that meeting, I found out the number of the victims involved. However, last year in January we had a meeting of the Helsinki Committee, and I found out about the killings in the village of Zecovi where women and children were killed. The son of one of these women spoke about this. Actually, he came from a family where the mother and her daughters - his sisters, that is - had been killed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You mean murdered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, those who were not murdered in those villages that had attacked the Serb forces, those women, children, and elderly, who again were not killed, could they remain in those villages? Did they continue to live there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really cannot give you an answer to that question as I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you ever hear anything about children and women being taken from their villages and held in a situation in which they were not entirely free to move around?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did hear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, when I -- you talked about the killing, you spontaneously answered by saying what you heard. Here you say, "I can't say anything about it," although you heard about it as well. What did you hear?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard about camps, if that's what we mean. Of course I heard about that. I heard about Omarska, Trnopolje, Keraterm. I heard about all of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zec, are you ready to start your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. You'll find him to your right. And Mr. Zec is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do so, can I ask a follow-up question on the questions by the Presiding Judge. Madam, you talked about women and children being murdered in the village of Zecovi. Can you tell us by whom were these people murdered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I see now that people are being arrested, people who had been killing these women and children in the village of Zecovi. As far as I know, already 16 of them were brought in; that is to say, Serbs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 16 of them were Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Do you know how many have been brought of whom the 16 form a part?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. Maybe -- I don't know the exact number, no. I know that quite a few Serbs were held accountable and were sentenced to many years in prison. Now, these arrests only have to do with the village of Zecovi as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Were these Serbs part of any army at the time when they killed, according to the allegations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know exactly now that they belonged to an army. I know about two men that I know personally. I heard that they had been arrested, that they were on the reserve police force. As for the others, I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The reserve police force of which army, of which authority?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Reserve policemen of the Serb authorities. The reserve police, the Serb reserve police.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- yes, but, Mr. Zec, to start cross-examination for three minutes might not be the wisest thing to do. Perhaps we take an early break, and we'd -- one second, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll not start your cross-examination before the break. We'd like to see you back in approximately 25 minutes from now. You may follow the usher. Meanwhile, I use the time until 10.30 for a short agenda item.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which is the following. It's about 92 ter motions for four witnesses: Bosiljka Mladic, Radovan Popovic, Biljana Stojkovic, and Zarko Stojkovic. On the 19th of December of last year, the Defence filed 92 ter motions for witnesses Bosiljka Mladic, Radovan Popovic, Biljana Stojkovic, and Zarko Stojkovic. The Prosecution does not oppose the motions. The Chamber has reviewed the motions and observes that there's a considerable amount of overlap between the witnesses' proposed evidence and the parties' joint submissions on agreed facts dated the 4th of June, 2013. In particular, these witnesses' testimonies relate directly to the chronology of the accused's whereabouts between the 14th and the 17th of July, 1995. Could the Defence please indicate why it is necessary to present evidence in relation to facts that have already been agreed between the parties? Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. First of all, there was a disagreement in between the parties about the moment of return of General Mladic to Republika Srpska. We have a disagreement on this issue. And also the Prosecution, through the Witness Lesic and his video recording, actually, is trying to present that General Mladic was able to command over the forces, although being outside the area of his responsibility and outside of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and we think it's crucial for us to prove that he did not have any means of communication by which he was or would be able to command his forces. And it is crucial for us to prove that on the 16th of July he was not in the area of Republika Srpska. So if we can agree on those two issues with the Prosecution, we would certainly not bring these witnesses to testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I do understand you well, there are three items which are in dispute. The first is technical possibilities for communication where Mr. Mladic was in Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one. Second, the exact time of his return.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And the third one, his whereabouts on the 16th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. We'll -- having this in mind, we'll re-read the statement and we'll see whether the statement focuses on that or whether it's more, because the presentation of evidence, and we'll also of course look at what the Prosecution witnesses said about it, the presentation of evidence should be focused on matters that are in dispute. But at least it's clear now which three points specifically caused you to introduce these 92 ter witness statements. We'll take a break and we'll resume at 10 minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Earlier this morning, we discussed P3758. I said that the B/C/S version should be replaced by the newly uploaded B/C/S version. Now, the newly uploaded version is a complete version; that is, both B/C/S, which is now -- in the version is put in the correct order. But it also contains the English version, which is unchanged. So, therefore, when I said that the B/C/S version should be replaced, I was not entirely accurate because the whole of the document is to be replaced, although the English version did not undergo any changes. I briefly deal with number -- the -- an item about the testimony of Radovan Glogovac. On the 4th of September of last year, Exhibit P6723 was marked for identification due to its length, and that can be found at transcript pages 25304. The Chamber was informed via an e-mail on the 17th of December by the Prosecution that an excerpt of the document has been uploaded into e-court under Rule 65 ter number 19313a.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are there any objections against the short version now uploaded to be admitted? Mr. Lukic is nodding that there is no objection. The Chamber hereby admits the excerpt uploaded under Rule 65 ter number 19313a as Exhibit P6723, and Madam Registrar is instructed to replace the current document in e-court with the excerpt bearing Rule 65 ter 19313a. Mr. Zec, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. Witness, I already told you that you would be cross-examined by Mr. Zec. You find him to your right. Mr. Zec, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And good morning, Ms. Karlica.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Just before the break, you were talking about what you learned during a conference about the killings in Zecovi. Can you just confirm for the clarity of the record that Zecovi is a village in Bircani area, which is part of Brdo, near Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in answering the question of His Honour, Judge Moloto, you referred to two men that you knew personally that were arrested in regard to this murder. Can you tell us the names of these two people?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Radomir Stojanic and his son Zoran.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And these people that were arrested, that happened just last year; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now with respect to your statement, you told us that you work as the president of the organisation for the families of captured and fallen soldiers and missing civilians of Prijedor. I will have just two quick questions about this. First, this organisation was part -- is part of the republican organisation for the families of captured and fallen soldiers and missing civilians of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Now without going into any detail about the work or the policy of the organisation, can you confirm that its main focus is tracking missing soldiers of the VRS and Serb civilians of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In your statement you talk about your late husband, Zdravko Karlica, and his combat activities. Your late husband, Ms. Karlica, he was honoured by the Serb -- by the RS authorities for his service and accomplishments as a loyal VRS soldier, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Just a brief observation, he's Zoran, not Zdravko.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: My apologies. That's my mistake. Can you confirm -- yes.

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: You spoke about this to Croatian -- yes, yes. He was the recipient of a decoration. And, that is to say, after his death.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The RS authorities have honoured your late husband for his war efforts by naming a square in Prijedor after him; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You say in your statement that your late husband was a member of the Prijedor Motorised Brigade as of September 1991 when he went to Croatia. In paragraph 3 you say, and I will quote: "My late husband told me that his task in Western Slavonia was to defend the Serbian people and of course our houses." So your late husband's position was that the Prijedor Motorised Brigade went to Croatia to protect the Serbian population in its entirety; that is, both those in Croatia and in Bosnia, yes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In paragraph 6, you say that Serbs in Prijedor started talking about the genocide committed against the Serbs during the Second World War, and in fact the public perception as communicated through the media was that the Serbian population was endangered by others and that the events of the Second World War were about to repeat; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Well, that's what people were saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: During the war, the Prijedor Motorised Brigade was praised in the media in Republika Srpska for its role in helping Serbs in Croatia for liberating Prijedor and saving the Serbian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't quite understand what you were saying, actually. They were members of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, and you know the date up until which that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this Chamber has received evidence about transformation from JNA to VRS, but my question was simpler than that. It's more about praising the war efforts of this brigade in Croatia and Bosnia. So their war efforts, they were praised in the media in Republika Srpska during the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And the RS authorities considered the liberation of Prijedor as important military victory; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Well, certainly, yes. I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I'll show you now a video-clip which was played on the Serbian television in 1994 which talks about a warpath and successes of the Prijedor Motorised Brigade. It may be that you have seen this video before, but I want to tell you that this video refers to your late husband, among other things. So I want you to know what is coming up in the video before it is being played. Is that okay for you?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, any text spoken? Do we have to play it twice?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, there is text spoken and we have asked CLSS to check the accuracy of the translation, which they kindly did. So I suggest that we play only once.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. I take it the accuracy of the transcription, that's in the original, and then we have to play it only once. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: For the record, the video is 65 ter 22733a.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: "[Voiceover] In fact, that was the best Serbian brigade in the period between the last two Saint Vitus's Days. This is the reason why the president of the republic, Dr. Radovan Karadzic, decorated the Prijedor men with the highest award of the state - the Nemanjic Order. The brigade was established on the 16th of September, 1991 by the order on mobilisation of what was then the 5th Banja Luka Corps of the Yugoslav Peoples' Army, and it became the 343rd Motorised Brigade of the Yugoslav Army. Within only two days, the brigade command managed to carry out the mobilisation and head out, with just 42 per cent of the necessary manpower and without any reinforcements to carry out a combat task on the main axis of the then-5th Banja Luka Corps. This axis was: Strug-Okucani-Lipik-Pakrac. "At that time, it was the Muslims or, rather, the Party of Democratic Action who held power in Prijedor. Their leadership did everything possible to prevent mobilisation, and especially to prevent the brigade from going to the front line and assisting the endangered Serbian people of Western Slavonia. They did so publicly, using threats, openly advocating secession and the creation of the Muslim Jamahiriya in the entire territory of the former Bosnia-Herzegovina. The warpath of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, better known and famous under the name of Prijedor Brigade, is not easy to describe because this brigade is special, unique and great in many ways, and it will certainly go down in Serbian war history as the brigade which won the swiftest, greatest, and most important victory in this battle - the battle for Prijedor. This battle and victory determined not only the fate of this town, but also the fate of the entire Serb people in Potkozarje and Krajina. "Potkozarje was and will remain a chapter that stands out; because it must not be forgotten that it was along this part of the centuries-old Serbian border - in this area populated by the best, the most honourable Serbs who ever lived and fought - that the mission to wipe out Serbdom had nearly been accomplished during and especially after the Second World War. Few and far between were any places where the wail of the muezzin would be answered by a chime from the belfry; few and far between were spots where incense still burned under the icon lamp. The Serb people of Potkozarje had been driven to their wits' end. They were at the end of their tether, at the mercy of reformists of all hues, peace-keepers, and newfangled democrats. Although at their wit's end, the Serbs were wary. At the eleventh hour, memories awakened of their bitter experience from the time of their great ordeal - the time of death, slaughter, genocide and extermination - but also the resolve not to let history repeat itself; the resolve to prevent a new massacre and another struggle for survival, at the price of seeing victory replaced by defeat, former executioners taking place of victims, the faith of their forefathers ceding to the nightmarish ideology of uniform thinking devised by Broz. "This is why on the 16th of September, Vladimir Arsic and his deputy, Radmilo Zeljaja, the commander and the Chief of Staff of the 43rd Motorised Brigade, respectively, took their units down a long road of trial and tribulation, uncertainty, tempering by fire and great victories. The first and perhaps the most triumphant" --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this still going on? I have nothing now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: We are continuing with the translation of the video. "At first and perhaps the most triumphant decisive victory of this brigade and the men of Kozara was precisely that battle in Western Slavonia. This was a time when its scout company, later name Zoran Karlica, after its celebrated commander, bore the brunt of the fighting in defence of its people and this part of the front line. With his young men, he seemed to be everywhere at once, closing gaps opened up after some parts of the units had pulled out. Very often, the scouts took on the enemy head-on, inflicting losses and sowing panic in their ranks."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, apologies for the delay. We were receiving translation what you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Wait. Yes. We were still waiting for the French translation to be finished. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We heard here, Ms. Karlica, among other things, that President Radovan Karadzic decorated the Prijedor Brigade with the highest award for their war efforts, including the most important victory of the war, the battle for Prijedor. So this reflects the importance of the victory and taking control over Prijedor to the RS leadership; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I have to say, if I may that is, that in the 43rd Brigade there were a lot of non-Serb soldiers, and I'm sure that the decoration was bestowed in the way described in the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And for the sake of better understanding of the video, I'll just -- I'll quickly ask you couple of quick questions. While the video was played, we saw the logo SRT. Can you confirm that this was the logo of the Serbian Radio Television which was the public media service of Republika Srpska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I was in two minds whether it was Serbia or Republika Srpska. It was a bit blurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Would you like to see again quickly to be -- to check or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Stop here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you see the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, is the issue you're raising whether this was Serb-oriented broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And to make clear that this was the public media service of Republika Srpska, and in that regard we have also a decision forming this media service by Republika Srpska Assembly we can offer if the Chamber would like to have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But -- yes, but apparently you want to emphasize that it's not neutral?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Well, whether it's Serb or Republika Srpska, in both cases you would say that it's at least -- but I'll let you go, if you would think it's -- it's really important for us to know that it was Republika Srpska television, then ... Also a matter, have you sought the agreement of the Defence on that matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: No, Mr. President. But perhaps we can talk or if they have position now, I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any challenge to this being a Republika Srpska public broadcasting?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I believe that that was indeed the case and that the symbol denotes the first year of work of the television of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, well, what you believe is not relevant for us. It is what you stipulate and agree upon is. You agree that it's Serb public -- Republika Srpska public broadcast?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, thank you, Mr. Stojanovic. Now going back to the video, and if we can have transcripts on the screen. 65 ter 22733a.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And very quick two questions, Ms. Karlica. If you look towards the end of the page in your language, you will see that there is a reference to the battle for Prijedor. And if you look that part towards the end of the page, a few lines, you will see there it says, and I will quote, if it's easier for you: "Few and far between were any places where the wail of muezzins would be answered by the chime from the belfry; few and far between were spots where incense still burned under the icon lamp." So it may be clear, but in your understanding does this mean, as it is presented here, that the non-Serb religious sites dominated over the Serb or Orthodox religious sites and its tradition; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, I am sure that there were more non-Serb religious facilities than those belonging to the Serbs, and I'm talking about a period preceding the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And if you look back at the transcript, starting from the place where we stopped.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we will need in B/C/S next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Looking over the first several lines --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then we have to go to the next page in English, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's correct. In B/C/S, we need previous page and next page in English; correct. Thank you very much. If we can in B/C/S -- if we can have page 1. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: You will see there is a reference, and I'll quote for you -- for your benefit. It just says: "... the nightmarish ideology of uniform thinking devised by Broz." So can you just confirm that this reference is -- refers to the time of Yugoslavia and the rule of socialism under Josip Broz Tito; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: It seems that I don't have the same text as you do. I can't find it. I'm not reading the same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S second page. My apologies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So first several lines you will see where it refers to the nightmarish ideology of the uniform thinking devised by Broz. So the question is simple: Do you agree that this is the reference to the socialism time of Yugoslavia and Josip Broz Tito?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The witness is asked to interpret somebody's words, the words that were not uttered by her, the words that she has nothing to do with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there any dispute as this is to be a reference to the -- to the socialism time of Yugoslavia? I mean ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Your Honours, as I'm reading this text, I can see that this has been taken from the context. That sentence has been misquoted by the Prosecutor, because that sentence actually reads: "The faith of our forefathers in what was construed to be Tito's ideology ..." But this is a free interpretation, so I am not in agreement what the Prosecutor is trying to imply here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, is there an interpretation issue? Then we should focus on the interpretation. Are you saying that it has to be verified, the interpretation? Is it not accurate?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, this is not what I'm claiming, Your Honours. I'm saying and I'm reading the text in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now the text you read and the text which was quoted by Mr. Zec -- just --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know that. I don't have that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Don't worry for a moment, Witness. Is that a reference to the -- a reference to the socialist time in which Tito was in power?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I cannot see that, Your Honours. And this, bearing in mind page 33, lines 2 and 3, on our today's record and the text of the question is precisely what we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: For the benefit of Mr. Stojanovic, if he reads line 6, there is a reference to Broz, and I'm referring to B/C/S line 6. There is a reference to Broz, and I think it's going to be clear then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Zec, the part you read in English is the last sentence of the first half of the page, isn't it, what we have on our screen now?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Where do we see that in -- let me just have a look.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, it's line 6 and Broz has a small capital.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So that's maybe confusing, because of the construction of that sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now you literally quote, because there apparently is no translation issue as far as Mr. Stojanovic is concerned, you literally quote, to start with, what you wanted to put to the witness and don't ask a question yet. Could you please quote exactly what you wanted to refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Simply the line where it refers to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, I asked you to read that line.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: "... nightmarish ideology of uniform thinking devised by Broz."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And you're the issue was whether this is a reference to the socialist time -- and, no, it was the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Under Josip Broz Tito; correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Any dispute about that, Mr. Stojanovic? A reference to an ideology developed or -- by Tito, wouldn't that be a reference to the time when he was in power? Or is there any other explanation you think is appropriate in this context?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Tito's ideology does not go just back to the period of socialism. It goes back to the 1930s when Tito became the leader of the Communist Party, from the fourth congress of the communist party that is. The question therefore is of an academic nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, first of all, it didn't change when he was in power after the 1930s, did it, in your view -- in the Defence's view? He didn't give up on that ideology later when he was in power, in the Defence's opinion?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think so. Although, after 1948 his policies evolved and took a different turn after the conflict with informbiro.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It seems it takes a course which is not for a witness to further interpret. We all know that there was a time, and that apparently is the -- we know when Tito was in power, at least the parties could agree on that, and that apparently this is a reference to his ideology. So I don't need -- see why we need the witness to further interpret this text.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I agree, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And we can move on. And I'll just tender this video and the Chamber will have an opportunity to review it on its own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the video which is now, I see, a DVD is given to the Registry. The number would be, Madam Registrar?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 22733a receives number P7028, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: In the absence of any objections, admitted into evidence. Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, we just heard the position of the Serb authorities regarding the importance of the victory in Prijedor. And in fact, after the take-over by Serb authorities, many of the street names and names of the schools in Prijedor were changed from non-Serb names and the names of communists to Serb names; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I know that that was the case. Some schools did change their names, and some streets did as well, except for the square and a couple streets that were named after the figures from the previous war.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: An example of that is the square in the city centre which it was called Lenin square, it was renamed to the name of your late husband. The street where you lived was called Marsala Tita Street was renamed to Kralja Petra I Oslobodioca Street; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: The name of the street is the street of King Peter the 1st, the liberator, if that's the street you had in mind. In the centre of the city; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. And I'll show you quickly one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: It's 65 ter 31650.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And this is a list of old and the new names of the streets and schools in Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there any dispute about massive changing of the names of streets? We've seen that in Serb and in non-Serb territories as well. Is there any dispute about it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If the Defence has no dispute, I think I can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And apart from what the relevance is. I mean, I do see that after a war that often peoples are inclined to rename and to get rid of what they consider a past which they would like not to be reminded of and then change that. And why do we have to go through all of these details? I mean, we have seen already so much dubious -- evidence of dubious relevance in the statement itself, and now to have in cross-examination even more of that is not something that the Chamber would encourage. You have not sought even the agreement of the Defence in that. Is there any agreement that changes -- or massively changed, Mr. Stojanovic, the names of the streets?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with this, Your Honours. A lot of the street names were indeed changed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, in your statement in paragraph 18 you gave an example of Puharska and Cela as an example that no one bothered non-Serbs and nobody touched any of the inhabitants. So basically, are you saying that there is no -- there was no instances of attacks, intimidations, killings, in these areas? And I'm referring to Puharska now for the example that you gave. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That's what I heard. Those villages were calm. There were no attacks. At least according to what I heard. If things happened differently, then I've been misinformed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The mosque in Donja --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we do that, who told you about Puharska, about what happened there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Drasko Vujic who was a witness here as well. He was there and he said that nothing was going on there. He was one of the commanders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When did he tell you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know. It was a long time ago, perhaps ten years or so. That's when he spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: The mosque in Donja Puharska was destroyed in summer 1992. In the explosion, several non-Serbs were killed and injured in their homes; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I know that happened. My sister lives nearby. I know that the house was damaged. I don't know that anybody was killed. I don't know or I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: During the course of the same evening when the mosque was destroyed, the Prijedor Catholic church was destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter 31821. And this is an investigative file regarding the destruction of the mosque in Donja Puharska. It contains the statement of Rasim Dzafic and several photographs of the mosque destroyed in 1992. Can we have e-court page 3 for the B/C/S and page 4 for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look at the last two paragraphs in your language, Ms. Karlica --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And in the English it's the first part of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- Dzafic said that he was injured in the explosion, that the Kusturan family members were killed while their son, Osman, was injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we now turn to the next page in the B/C/S and then in the English as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Looking at the second-last paragraph in the statement, it says that the course of the same evening the Catholic church was destroyed. And I'll just quickly show you the photographs that are in this file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if we can both --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, if the witness could tell us anything about it, then we would like to hear. But just to inform the witness about what was reported at the time, if she says she has no knowledge about it, it doesn't make any sense -- Witness, it's now put to you that the Puharska population was not untouched, that the mosque was destroyed, and this caused victims. Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Puharska is a rather wide area. When I said that it was calm there, I had in mind the area behind the Zarko Zgonjanin Barracks. As for Donja Puharska, where the mosque was demolished and some 400 or 500 metres away was that church, I heard about those incidents. Actually, those were very powerful explosions that we all heard. At that time I resided in Urije and I heard the explosion. When I spoke about Puharska, I had in mind the part of the Puharska behind the barracks. Not Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, would you agree that if a mosque was blown up in Puharska, Donja Puharska, that that would have touched upon the non-Serb population of that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There was Serb and non-Serb population there. The mosque was close to the city. It's not a village. It's actually a suburb of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I didn't talk about ethnicity. I was just talking about whether it touched upon the population irrespective of their ethnicity. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course. We were all upset that a thing like that had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, that's not expressed in your statement, but I do understand that that's limited to a very small area which is not the whole of the Puharska area. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Did you know that people of Puharska were taken and killed; an example, Fadil Dizdarevic who was taken and shot. Did you know about that example?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the family name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I gave the example Fadil Dizdarevic. He was taken and shot?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: If you look at the statement in front of you in B/C/S page 3, English page 4, e-court page 4 in English -- and then we --

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: It's page 2 on my screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In B/C/S, next page. B/C/S -- next page in B/C/S, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if you look at around the middle of the first paragraph, and it's -- it says: "Several days later, our neighbour, Fadil Dizdarevic, came to repair hodza's house. Djordje Dosen, also known as Djo [phoen], found him there. He took him to the car and drove off. A day or two later, Fadil's body was found in the Sana River. His chest was riddled with bullets." So this is an example of what was happening to people, non-Serb population of Puharska; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I am really not in a position to know that. You know that my husband succumbed to his wound on the 6th of June. I don't know when this happened, though. For a year, there was not a single day that I didn't go to the cemetery to visit my husband's grave. How was I supposed to know this? If I'd been in the neighbourhood, perhaps I would have known. But really I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, the reason why Mr. Zec is asking you is because you give in your statement a comment on what happened in Cela and Puharska, whereas you said you heard that some ten years ago. Now, what Mr. Zec is doing is asking you some details which he finds in documents, and I do understand that your answer is that you had no personal knowledge about many events which may have taken place in that area. That's the issue Mr. Zec is raising and he has done so. Please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would tender this file with photographs. If you would like me to go with witness through the photograph, if she recognise, if it's helpful for the Chamber, we can do it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is there --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: There is no need to have the witness identify the -- if there is any serious concerns about these photographs depicting something which is not depicting what it is said to depict, then we would like to hear from the Defence without any delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We shall object to have this admitted into evidence, particularly because it is complex. It consists of a statement by a witness and a few photographs for the area of Donja Puharska as is written here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And if a document is complex, is that a reason to have it not admitted, Mr. Stojanovic? Any basis for that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, from the very outset it has been our position that witnesses who do not appear here should not have their statements admitted. A person is not being called here and then this is being tendered nevertheless. Also, this is documentation that was compiled on the 5th of September, 1997 by the Ministry of Police and the Security Services Centre in Bihac. That's what is stated here. So the authenticity of this document is questionable, therefore. It is for all these reasons that we believe that this should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The one and only matter that remains as relevant for our decision, whether or not to admit, is the authenticity. And, Mr. Stojanovic, authenticity of what exactly? It not being a -- the document created in 1997, or the photographs not depicting what they are supposed to depict? What's, exactly, the authenticity issue you raise so that Mr. Zec has an opportunity to tackle it or to accept it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, according to this document, photographs were taken in September 1992 which would indicate that this happened in September 1992 at the latest. The photographs and this document, nevertheless, were compiled by a completely different organ from a different town, the CSB in Bihac, on the 5th of September in Bihac, 1997. So we don't have the chain, we don't have any information about how this reached Bihac all of a sudden. So all that brings into question the authenticity of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, irrespective of the fact whether what you raised a second ago is a thorough challenge to the authenticity, because the fact that photographs are taken in 1992 does not automatically mean that they only are accurate or if they are put in a document in 1992. But, Mr. Zec, you have an opportunity to ask further questions about the photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And only to note, Mr. President, the reason I tendered the whole file is that the statement explains the destruction of the mosque and the chain of custody of the photographs in the file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So that's helpful. And I can certainly provide additional information when we received this file.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, if you want to put any further questions to the witness in relation to the photographs, you have an opportunity to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, let's quickly look these photographs, and I'll ask you if you can recognise their location and the mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So if we can have now in B/C/S and English next page. In English, we should also have -- next page in English. One more page, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, in English there are no photographs.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But perhaps the text, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct. Yes, there is the translation of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So this is the mosque in Puharska before it was destroyed. Can you recognise?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I recognise that this is a mosque. But, please, may I be allowed to say something? Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. Witness, you earlier testified that your sister was living quite close to this mosque, I take it. That question was about the same mosque, Mr. Zec. Do you recognise this mosque as the mosque which was close to where your sister lived?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, it is that mosque. But please, may we clarify one thing: This is Donja Puharska, whereas I spoke about Puharska. I did not speak about Donja Puharska and you keep leading me to -- these are two different places.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That has been clarified previously and it clearly says, under this photograph as well, that is Donja Puharska. So that is -- there is no doubt about that. So please proceed, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page in English and B/C/S. Perhaps we can see also next page with -- they are similar, so we can then -- I will ask the witness if she can recognise. Can we have next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise this as remains of the mosque in Puharska after this destruction?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should clarify Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I see it as D Puharska.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: In Donja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And can we have the English translation of what is being said on this picture, please? Because I think that this related to the previous picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Perhaps we can also go to next page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, let's --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- first see whether the witness can answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps you repeat the question so that the witness is reminded of what it was about.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, are you able to recognise this as remains of the mosque, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I cannot challenge this, but I myself had not seen this in this state. I never went there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness had looked at page 7 of the B/C/S in this report. Page 7 in e-court. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we turn next page. Again, next page. Again, next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So on this page, we see the utility company of Prijedor clearing the remains of the mosque. Are you able to recognise anything and were you aware that the public utility company of Prijedor was clearing the sites of this destroyed mosque?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: No, really. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness was looking at page 10 in e-court of this document. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can we turn the page. This is page 11, depicting the house of Rasim Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise the house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I cannot. Because my sister, I mean, as the crow flies --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, you cannot recognise it. That was the question. You've answered that question. Please proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have next page, and I believe we are now page 11 -- page 12. And this is depicting the house of Zekerijah Kusturan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Can you recognise this house?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Again, depicting the house of Rasim Dzafic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Are you able to recognise this?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And I believe we have one more photograph at next page. Or that was the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, only to now clarify the Donja Puharska and Gornja Puharska. So these are the two places. The one, Donja Puharska, was closer to the town, and Gornja Puharska was a bit further from the town in same direction; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: How far would you say is from Donja Puharska to Gornja Puharska?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: I could not really give a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Your Honours, in evidence we have map P1 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. -- what was your time estimate, Mr. Zec.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: 45 minutes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 45 minutes. You are far beyond that, isn't it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And -- so would you please -- it was time for a break anyhow. Would you please conclude. I mean, if the witness says that she never observed the place after the destruction, then to go through all the details and to hear the no, no, no answers that is -- of course, not, there are other matters as well which may affect the efficiency of your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Mr. President, the reason I went through the photographs is the Defence objection on the admission of the file. I was hoping the witness can help us in the sense that she can recognise the area and confirm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- the information in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. She was unable to do so and she made that clear when she answered the question that she had never seen that place after the destruction. Let's move on. If you could please try to conclude within the next two or three minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I will try, Mr. President. And if I only tender this file into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. The -- still a challenge to authenticity, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Any further details?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, especially not these -- after these questions were put to the witness and she could not recognise any of this or see herself in the context of Gornja Puharska.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The admission is denied, Mr. Zec. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Ms. Karlica, in paragraph 12 you say that it's well known that in mid-May 1992 there were over 2000 -- more precisely, 2.172 members of the Kozarac -- members of the TO in Kozarac, and you referred to a military expert in the trial of Aleskic and Cerkic in 2014. First, did you know this military expert that you referred to?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So can we have quickly 65 ter 2559j.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: So what we will be looking at is a 1991 census of Prijedor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: We need page 4. At page 4, we will see there is a -- Kozarac in line 36. So we will need next page in B/C/S, following line 36.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: And it says that Kozarac in 1991 had 4.045 people in total, which includes everyone, women, children, men, elderly, Serbs, Muslims, and the number of Muslims was 3.740. So do you agree that nearly two-thirds of the Kozarac population could not be members of the TO and the figure you cited in your statement, paragraph 12 of your statement, is an error; right?

utterances.speaker: ZDRAVKA KARLICA
utterances.text: That is not an error because Mr. Sadirlija stated that at the trial that was attended by representatives of our organisation because I could not attend personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: I tender this census, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The whole of the ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Four pages --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: -- for Prijedor only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Four pages for Prijedor only. Any objections? Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are the four pages uploaded as one document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: They should be. Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 2559j receives number P7029, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZEC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Your Honours, nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Zec. We'll take a break. Would you have any questions after the break, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then in that situation, we would already excuse the witness. Ms. Karlica, since the Defence has no further questions for you, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you, put to you by the parties, put to you by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We take a break and will resume at 12.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Kalabic, I take it. Mr. Kalabic, before you give evidence the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kalabic. Please be seated. Mr. Kalabic, you'll first be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You find him to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic. Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir. Can you please state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Rajko Kalabic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can please have document 1D01617 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I would direct your attention to the left side of the monitor and ask you if you could tell us whose signature is visible on the first page of this document?

utterances.speaker: RAJKO KALABIC
utterances.text: The signature on the first page of this document is mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And if we could turn to the last page of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
